opus-5.5.text:
I'm quite optimistic, but I think the more interesting question is less *whether* it will happen and more *what shape* it will take.

On whether it's possible: I think it's very likely. Computers and phones are a natural environment for agents. Everything is digital, the action space is defined (clicking, typing, calling APIs, writing code), and a huge share of human economic activity already happens there. Compared with robotics, where you fight the physical world, the digital world is far more tractable. Language models gave us strong priors and reasoning, so the remaining gap is less about raw intelligence and more about reliability, long-horizon execution, memory, and learning from feedback in real environments.

But I'd push back a little on the framing of "nearly any task." What makes a task hard for an agent often isn't the difficulty of each step but the context. A human assistant who has worked with you for three years knows your preferences, your accounts, which emails matter, and what "book me a reasonable flight" means to you. The model can be smart, but without that context it's like a brilliant new hire on day one. So I think the real bottleneck is shifting from capability to context and trust: how the agent gets the right information, how it interacts with the user, and when it should act versus ask.

There's also an interface question. Today a lot of work goes into making agents operate GUIs built for humans, clicking buttons and reading screens. That's a useful bridge, and it lets agents work with the existing world immediately. But long term, I suspect much of the environment will reshape itself around agents: more APIs, more structured interfaces, maybe new kinds of apps designed for AI to use. The agent changes the computer, and the computer changes the agent.

And then there's evaluation and utility. For a long time the field optimized benchmarks: solve this math problem, pass this test. When you move to real computer tasks, the question becomes whether it actually creates value for a real person. That's a different game. You need tasks that reflect real work, reward signals that aren't trivially hackable, and products where people come back to the agent because it saves them time.

So my overall assessment: the general digital agent is coming, maybe faster than many expect in narrow but valuable domains like coding and research, and more gradually in messy everyday tasks where context and trust matter most. I don't think it will arrive as one magic moment. It will be a steady expansion of what we're comfortable delegating, and the companies and researchers who define good environments, good tasks, and good human–agent interaction will shape what "general" ends up meaning.

r001.rationale: The response says the digital action space is defined and discusses tasks being difficult because of missing context, but it does not state that agent operation depends on whether the requested tasks can be reasonably defined.

r002.rationale: It describes a human assistant benefiting from accumulated knowledge of a user's preferences and accounts, but does not identify acquiring context as often the hardest problem for humans.

r003.rationale: The response says the remaining gap is less about raw intelligence and describes agents as smart but limited without context, naming context and trust as bottlenecks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting directions right now, but I want to be careful about separating what's inevitable from what's hard.

The inevitable part is the interface. A general agent operating a computer or phone the way a person does is attractive precisely because you don't have to rebuild the world for it. Every piece of software, every website, every app was designed for a human with eyes and hands. If you can give a model a screen, a keyboard, a mouse, and the ability to look, act, and look again, then in principle the whole digital world becomes its action space. That's the appeal, and it's why so many people, including me, think it will happen.

The hard part is that this action space is enormous and very unforgiving. When I was working on ReAct and later WebShop, the lesson that kept coming back was that reasoning and acting have to be interleaved. You can't plan everything up front, because the environment keeps surprising you. A button is somewhere else, a page hasn't loaded, a popup appears. Humans handle this almost without thinking, but for a model, each of those moments is a chance to drift off course, and in a long task the errors compound. Doing one step at ninety-five percent accuracy sounds good until you need fifty steps in a row.

So I think the question of "a general agent on computers and phones" is actually a question about three things. First, perception and grounding: can the model reliably read a screen and map intent to a concrete click or keystroke. That's improving fast with multimodal models. Second, long-horizon reliability: can it recover when something goes wrong instead of spiraling. That's where I think most of the remaining gap is. Third, and this is what I feel most strongly about, evaluation. We've spent a decade building benchmarks for language, but we barely have good environments that measure whether an agent can actually finish real tasks. SWE-bench, tau-bench, things like OSWorld, these are a start, but we need much more of this. In my view, the bottleneck for agents is not the model, it's the environment and the evaluation. Once you can measure something well and let the model interact with it at scale, progress tends to follow quickly.

My honest timeline is that narrow versions already work, things like filling forms, booking, routine software tasks in constrained settings. The broad version, where you hand over your laptop and it does whatever you'd do, I think is a matter of a few years rather than decades, but the last mile of reliability and trust will take longer than the demos suggest. And I'd add that when it does arrive, the interesting change isn't that computers get easier to use. It's that the unit of work shifts from "what can I do on this screen" to "what outcome do I want," and that reshapes how software itself gets designed.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the size of the action space and the need for better task environments and evaluation, but does not say agent ability depends on whether requested tasks can be reasonably defined.

r002.rationale: It does not identify acquiring context or background as often the hardest problem for humans.

r003.rationale: It names long-horizon reliability and environment/evaluation as bottlenecks, but does not identify incomplete context as a frequent bottleneck for current models.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very promising direction, but there’s a big difference between an agent that can attempt almost any task and one that can reliably complete almost any task. Computers and phones give us a fairly general interface to the digital world. If an agent can understand what’s on the screen and operate those interfaces, it can potentially work across many applications. But having access to that interface doesn’t automatically give it the judgment to use it well.

The hard part is sustaining reliable behavior over a long sequence of actions. An agent might handle each individual step reasonably well, but a task can involve dozens or hundreds of steps. It needs to notice when something has gone wrong, recover, and determine whether it has actually achieved the user’s goal. Sometimes it also needs to recognize that the user’s request is ambiguous and ask a question.

So I would expect progress to be gradual. We’ll first see agents become genuinely useful for tasks where the goal is clear and the result is easy to verify. Their scope can expand as their reliability improves. A demonstration where an agent successfully completes a complicated task is exciting, but for everyday use, I care more about whether I can delegate that task repeatedly without having to watch every action. That’s the gap we need to close.

r001.rationale: The response says agents will be useful first when the goal is clear and their scope can expand as reliability improves, linking task definition to their ability to work across computer and phone applications.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss humans or identify acquiring context or background as their hardest problem.

r003.rationale: The response discusses reliability over long action sequences, but does not identify incomplete context as a frequent bottleneck for current AI models.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m optimistic about the direction, but I think “nearly any task” is a much higher bar than it first sounds. An agent might successfully book a restaurant or edit a spreadsheet in a demo, but a general agent has to handle unfamiliar interfaces, ambiguous instructions, unexpected errors, and tasks that take hundreds of steps. It also needs to recognize when it should ask you a question instead of making an assumption.

The key distinction is between being able to do something occasionally and being reliable enough that you can delegate it. If you have to watch every click, you haven’t really saved much work. So I would assess progress by how much useful work an agent can complete independently, including recovering when something goes wrong.

Computers and phones are attractive environments because so many tasks already happen there. But I don’t think the agent necessarily needs to interact exactly like a human. It can use an API when one is available and a graphical interface when necessary. What matters is completing the user’s goal.

I expect this to develop gradually: agents will become dependable within particular kinds of work, then handle broader tasks with less supervision. Getting to something you can trust with almost anything will require progress in reasoning, learning from feedback, and sustained interaction with the environment—not just better answers in a chat window.

r001.rationale: The response mentions ambiguous instructions and asking questions, but does not state that an agent’s ability to operate computers or phones depends on whether tasks are reasonably defined.

r002.rationale: It makes no claim about acquiring context or background being harder for humans than reasoning.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim that incomplete context is a frequent bottleneck for current AI models; it instead mentions reasoning, feedback, and sustained interaction as areas for progress.
